text: Every CloudWatch metric lives inside a namespace, and a dimension is what narrows that down to one specific thing you actually care about. Every CloudWatch Logs event, meanwhile, can be queried straight out of the box with Logs Insights, no index to build first. This lesson covers both halves: how metrics are organized, and how to actually write a Logs Insights query that answers a real operational question.

A namespace groups related metrics — AWS/EC2, AWS/Lambda, or a custom namespace like Checkout/Orders for your own application metrics. A metric name like CPUUtilization isn't specific enough alone, since EC2 publishes that name for every instance in your account. A dimension, a name-value pair like InstanceId equals a specific instance ID, narrows it to one real time series. Resolution is the third piece: standard resolution stores one point every 60 seconds by default, while high-resolution, published with StorageResolution set to 1, stores down to every second — at the cost of more PutMetricData traffic, so reach for it selectively.

Here's a baseline Logs Insights query: fields picks @timestamp and @message, filter narrows down to messages matching ERROR, sort puts the newest first, and limit caps it at 20 rows. That's the query you'd run the moment a metric alarm fires, to see what's actually showing up in the logs right now.

parse is where it gets powerful: it pulls a structured field — here, a bracketed severity level — straight out of an unstructured log line, so you can filter on level equals ERROR specifically rather than just the substring ERROR appearing anywhere. stats then aggregates: count those errors, bucketed into five-minute windows with bin, so you can see whether the error rate is actually climbing or just a one-off blip.

On the organization side: a log group is the top-level container, almost always scoped to one resource, like slash aws slash lambda slash checkout-function, and that's where you set a retention policy — log events never expire by default until you set one. Inside that group, a log stream holds events from exactly one source: one Lambda environment, one EC2 instance. A busy function writes many streams into the same group at once, which is exactly why Logs Insights queries run across the whole group, not one stream.

That's metrics and logs in CloudWatch: namespace, dimension, and resolution identify and tune a metric; log groups and log streams organize raw log data; and Logs Insights, with fields, filter, parse, and stats, turns that raw data into real answers. Next lesson takes those metrics further, into alarms — and specifically composite alarms, built to catch a real problem without flapping on every minor blip.
